As an Uber driver, good luck with that. If I'm driving at night, I'm carrying.

It seems a bit overconfident on Uber's part to think that they can really do this, legally and pragmatically.

If Uber can set any conditions at all on a contracted driver's behaviour then I don't see how they can't legally do this. Your car must be clean, you must wear pants, you must not carry a gun. Not an unreasonable set of conditions to put into the contract between Uber and its drivers.

As a practical matter, of course, it's unenforceable. They're not gonna send people out to search drivers for weapons. And if a driver does turn out to be carrying a weapon then I doubt there's much they can do in the way of legal penalties except say "naughty naughty, you're not driving for us again".
Why does Uber make this decision for drivers? Drivers own the cars they drive for Uber so shouldn't it be their say as to what is allowed in the car?

I can see both sides of the debate on whether or not they should allow legal guns in cars. That is a valid question, but I won't weight in on that right now.

What I will point out, instead, is that Uber is trying to have things both ways, setting policies as an employer while simultaneously claiming they are simply a facilitator, not an employer. Uber has claimed, consistently, that they do not employ the drivers, but instead they are merely an agent acting between clients and drivers. According to a recent ruling by the California Labor Commission, however, they are an employer since they control every facet of the ride operation, from hiring to ride coordination to what happens inside the vehicle. When Uber makes this sort of policy decision for all drivers and clients, it reinforces that ruling. If they truly are a facilitator, then the gun/no-gun issue is between the driver and the passenger. If, on the other hand, Uber makes this sort of ruling for the entire driver/client base, then they are acting as an employer by setting the policy.

In short, the issue (and the confusion) is that Uber is trying to act as an employer when they like, but then they deny that status when they choose to.

Honestly the only one that's really convenient is my fitness pal. Being able to easily track the nutritional values of what you eat is the most important part of staying fit. It's also one of the only reliable methods of monitoring fitness. Even though nutritional value is standardized, it still gives you a decent estimation of nutrients, whereas with exercise based monitoring there's simply too many factors that have significant potential for variance.

Feedback and a question:

Looks good. There seem to be a lot of users (so you would assume it's a good app!). I've taken a look at the app and there are all the standard features: goals, calorie counter, steps, barcode scanner etc. There's no water intake tracker as far as I can see, but to be honest that seems like a minor point that I could gloss over. There's also nothing about heart rate on there, so I would need to record and observe that on the fitbit app.

Now the question - if you want to track your exercise from a fitness band with these third party apps, does the official app have to be running? E.g. to get my data from fitbit to myfitnesspal, does the fitbit tracker app have to be running?

Thanks for your response!

Late to the convo: but I would suggest the Garmin Forerunner 220. It's had a price drop now that the 225 is out. It will track heart rate, all the useful distance and speed fields, but no steps. If steps are going to be essential, then there is the more stylish Vivoactive which will work as a decent smartwatch as well. And my personal favorite but total overkill watch would be the Fenix 3 which does all of the above and more.

EDIT: if you are looking to stay with something near the size of a fitbit: the Vivofit 2 will do chest strap HR, which is far more accurate than the wrist based monitoring. But it will lack GPS unlike the watches.
